“Shape Shifters of the Suburbs: The Boy from the Temple of Heaven” is the first in a series of tween/YA novels about Breccan, a young man who can change into any animal he wants, from a mouse to a dolphin to a wolf.His adopted mother, Mary, longed for a child and didn’t give up—and eventually China allowed her to adopt Breccan as a small child, saying that he had been abandoned because he was possessed by sorcery. As Breccan grows, he is forced to keep himself apart from others in case they find out about his gift—but by the time he reaches seventh grade he does have a few close friends, including Jackson, Serenity, and Sabel. Neither Serenity nor Sabel are entirely normal teens either, though, and soon the group forms a bond that will have to stand strong against a Wendigo and the nefarious Black Heart and Dagger Association. Along the way, Breccan learns more both about accepting himself and channeling his power; he’s not alone as a shape shifter in the world, which opens up a lot of possibilities for future adventures.I read a lot of YA, and I enjoyed “Shape Shifters” a lot—if I had read this book as a tween/YA, it would have been one of my favorites! (And as an adult I still thought it was great.) Breccan’s back story is creative and mysterious enough to propel you into the sequel; he’s also an excellent hero for the book. He’s smart and a good kid—his only angst is having a crush on Serenity when he knows Sabel likes him too, and I especially liked how close he was to his mother and how they had a respectful, nurturing bond with each other. Younger readers will also like the gentle romance between Serenity and Breccan, and be drawn to Sabel’s sassy, strong personality. Lucinda also makes an appropriately realistic villain, her jealousy and hate twisted into something dark and murderous. There’s also plenty of action in the plot, including Breccan exploring his powers, discovering other shifters, and even fighting for his life.In sum, “Shape Shifters of the Suburbs” is creative and engrossing, with an exciting plot that’s filled with action and likeable characters. Though the cover is a little off-putting and looks more like a werewolf horror story, that’s definitely not what lies between the covers! I would recommend it to readers who enjoy YA fantasy, especially urban fantasy series.
summary: Creative and Exciting YA Fantasy Filled with Magic and Action

I have been eagerly anticipating Chelsea Fine’s next contemporary since finishing Sophie & Carter, and I’m glad to report that Best Kind of Broken was so very worth the wait.I know. I read a new adult novel and actually liked it.For those of you who’ve stuck with the blog(or my Goodreads reviews) for a while (BTDubs, you’re awesome.), might know that I’m a bit disenchanted with the new adult genre. For some reason, that I can’t chalk up to anything more than being ridiculously stubborn, I keep trying to find ones I like. And though I’ve found a handful, more often than not I’ve found from book to book, it’s generally the SAME story being retold again and again with essentially the same character archetypes, with the romance and the schmexy times completely overshadowing any interesting character/relationship development and/or plot. (I know, I’m painting with a broad brush here, but this has been my own experience with the genre.)Where Best Kind of Broken excels for me is Chelsea’s strong characters who develop independently, as well as together, and her primary relationship focus being on the emotional. Sure there’s crackling romantic tension, but primarily this story is about two friends (who might’ve been more) estranged after a tragedy who are now forced to deal and duke it out with each other and all their unresolved, unaired issues. And Chelsea does this in a way that is beautifully funny, poignant, messy, sweet, spicy, tear-worthy, and yes, a bit smolderific as Pixie & Levi try to figure out how they’re supposed to live in the wake of their crippling loss. And this strong — and well done — emphasis on the individual healing of Pixie & Levi and the emotional relationship between the two of them made this book a winner for me.(Smolderific. That should totally be a word.)Told from both Pixie and Levi’s perspective, these are two characters (who feel like real people, instead of BTDT, cardboard stereotypes), with wonderfully unique voices that I connected with right off the bat. Both a bit broken, both of them stuck, both of them grieving, both of them stubborn and not exactly thrilled at being maneuvered into working with each other for the summer. And so, they try to avoid each other. At least, as much as that is possible when you share a bathroom. And when avoidance doesn’t work, annoyance. From their “hot water wars,” to learning to throw the perfect spiral, to “scruffy cheese,” to reappropriated Transformers and more, Chelsea also does a fantastic job of establishing their past history together — Levi’s family being a stand-in for Pixie’s own, then later as best friends, to “Status: Indefinable” — and as a result, their chemistry and interactions feel layered and organic.And the banter! Oh, the banter. There really is nothing like well-written, clever banter. Ermiright?Overall, if you’re looking for a new adult novel that deviates from the norm, with depth and fantastic characters (not to mention, great dialogue), I’d definitely recommend Best Kind of Broken.*** Due to mature content, I’d recommend this book for readers 18+***

Realising Blair was too young Sean sent him and his friends Holden and Maddox to Europe to finish school and then attend College and traveling.  It would allow Blair to become a man instead of a young Pup with no life experience.  Blair did not react well, he didn't want to go and then when he graduated from High School he wanted to come back. Sean wouldn't let him return until he finished College, another four years away. In retaliation Blair refused contact with Sean for four years...but now he is back in the fold and makes a beeline for his mate who had better not try to reject him again if he knows what is good for him.This series are linked short books that are well written, descriptive and entertaining. I love the loyalty of the brotherhood. I adore the possessiveness of the "You are mine" an "property" comments. These are all things I just love about rough romances. But what I am is chicken when it comes to relationship roughness. Meaning, angst. How they treat each other, how specifically the men treat the women. Nope I'm a big old fat angst chicken. I am also a romantic sap.  I loved so much of this book then I thought OH MY GOSH she's gonna DO IT! She's gonna give me just what I want. These two had scenes that literally took my breath away...I loved it ..I was on pins and needles wanting MORE MORE MORE. Shadow and Dani were growing on me by the second.But then I got knocked down on my ass and I wanted to cry.Everything that I might have disliked or had problems with is going to be just what makes this book SELL and makes this book ROCK because I know I'm in the minority.Most people love MC books because of the angst and the drama. I am the one that loves the ones where the guys are 100% loyal and so are the women. I can't stand it any other way. So just because parts of this story broke my heart doesn't mean it's not going to just blow some people away . I can almost guarantee it will.  I'm rating it on the romance story...just not my cup of tea..but on the writing and the ability to cause feelings of all passion, fear and anger..yea that is a solid 5. I've had the pleasure of talking to Ms. Forgy and she's the nicest and most down to earth lady I've talked to in a long time. I hope we work together a lot more in the future. I know I'll be seeing her name when this book starts hitting the kindles and ereaders. Written in a complex and passionate way this will be a fan of many hard care thrill seeking, angst filled, biker story junkies.*Copy offered for honest review

reviewText: Title: The Secrets They KeptAuthor: Charmaine GallowayPublisher: Charming Gal PublicationsSeries: Girl Friends Secrets Part 2Reviewed By: Arlena DeanRating: 5Review:"The Secrets They Kept" by Charmaine Galloway was the part two of this author's Girl Friends Secrets novel and was a wonderful read that picks up from the beginning for Tyra, Alisha and Brittany. These ladies really have or had some secrets that will really cause you to wonder...why and was it worth it all in the end because secrets seem to always come out in one form or another as you will see from the read. The three main characters: Tyra, Alisha and Brittany really went through quite a lot and one thing for sure the question will be asked and answered... will there be forgiveness for all in the end even thought none of them were perfect? "The Secrets They Kept" was indeed a read that will leave you with a 'spiritual message' in the end, definitely one that will leave you thinking about long after it has been read. What real life adversity will be taught from this read? One thing for sure it was through faith and belief yourself with God's help you can overcome any obstacle and have a better life. So, we have Tyra's situation ... how will it be handled? Then on to Alisha and Brittany...will they be able to work it out the situation that was holding them back from being best friends again? This is where I say you must pick up "The Secrets They Kept" to see how this author will bring it all out to the reader. I really loved the ending however, I was left really wondering about Tyra's son (Tyree) and I see that in this next authors' read we will get more in 'Tyree's Love Triangle." This is really a wonderful well written novel of triumph and what happens when you forgive. Would I recommend? YES, Yes!

This book is a wonderful read, dedicated to the spirit of Christmas and those who love it, and I was pleasantly surprised by how much I enjoyed it.The language of the story is soft and fuzzy reminiscent of those 90s movies we all watched as children i.e. everyone is beautiful, wholesome and good-natured. The descriptions of the snow and decorations, at Cindy and Trent's home in particular, are wonderful evoking images of a Victorian postcard or an Alpine village. Cindy herself is a sweet heroine, initially quite a tragic figure sitting alone in her Christmas cottage, she soon warms up and wins the readers' hearts by how game she is for an adventure - not many women would go meet a man's parents after meeting him for a whole three hours!The book is also really funny - there is a great moment when the young couple are looking for a certain absentee reindeer in the snow and Trent thinks that Cindy wants to split from him when she is really only suggesting they cover more ground to look for their missing animal friend. The sexuality of the novel is a little bizarre at times and is slightly at odds with the Christmas imagery as we swap between the two worlds of Christmas cheer and sexy passion very fast, but the scenes are well written so Scholl just about gets away with it. This story is part romance, part homage to Christmas, part sexy romp all rolled into one. An excellent way to spend an afternoon!Review by Eleanor Whalley on behalf of BestChickLit.com
summary: Sex, romance and Christmas all rolled into one!

Some of the rather bizarre plot twists are believable and serve the story well.The young American woman at the center of this novel, Yvonne, sets out to write a wrong by replacing a brass rubbing that is precious to her grandmother and which was destroyed in a fire caused by Yvonne. Along the way, she becomes involved with a different individuals who are struggling with broken relationships. In seeking to "put things right" in the lives of the people she meets and in her grandmother's life, she learns that sometimes "love conquers all" means the cost of restoring one relationship may mean destroying other relationships.The author's writing style makes this novel accessible to many different readers. However, there is a disconnect between the story itself and the philosophical reflection at the end. The author uses a rather simplistic writing style in the story, but a much more complex and nuanced style in the conclusion. Personally, I would have enjoyed the story even more if the author had found a middle ground between the two styles, end using more depth into the story itself..
summary: Good Read with Colorful Characters and  Unexpected Plot Twists

The Civil War saw thousands of Canadians enlisting to join the Americans in battle. Shared from the viewpoint of Jack Burns and his daughter Kitt, this beautifully touching novella relates the journey that both experience during the time of Jack's service. It also communicates both distinctly and figuratively, why many Canadians took up arms alongside their American neighbours.Kitt Burns has her heart so entwined with her Pappy's that she is present with him and his regiment in spirit; always encouraging and always inspiring. Kitt is staying on at her Pappy's farm in Chestnut, Nova Scotia, with her Aunt and Uncle. A profound and spiritual child, she can be found sitting in tall grass under peaceful blue skies while Janey her tabby cat wanders nearby; and can be seen deep in thought, lifting prayers to heaven, and frequently scribbling down inspired poetry with flair and an astute insight that continues to flourish as the days pass. Kitt's letters and poems to her Pappy bring light to an otherwise dark place on earth.Jack Burns is on the battlefield in western Tennessee with his regiment and other platoons waiting for orders. He's made a promise to Kitt that he will one day come walking down that winding dusty road toward his farm and his daughter, and he means to keep his promise. But to do that, the war needs to finish. And he will have to face an extremely dangerous attack against an impregnable Missionary Ridge as a step in that direction.Murray and Micaela Pura have together penned a mesmerizing and touching account of one of the most important battles in the history of the Civil War. Complimenting this compelling story are the pensive and discerning poems beautifully composed by Micaela. Highly recommended!
summary: Compelling account of the battle on Missionary Ridge!

Vic Bayne is a PsyCop. He's the psychic half of a detective team assigned to special cases where certain types of paranormal activity may be at work. Because Vic's a bit of a basket case, Jacob's doing the screening. It's tough to find a new place that's clean, convenient, affordable, and not haunted. Since his last partner kidnapped him and nearly killed him, he's now breaking in "Zig", an old-time cop that's Vic is not quite comfortable with yet. He also has to meet Jacob's relatives, and a string of missing persons cases is leading him down a darker and darker path.The writing style is addictive. The story interesting, witty, and very erotic at times. Characters are brought to life, and there are a few good chills to be had. The interplay between the characters is good, and their relationships are interesting and enjoyable to read. It's a very good supernatural tale with fresh and compelling characters.

reviewText: Inception is a novella that follows Ashley’s first book Mirage.  It tells Danny’s POV of things that happened in Mirage- How he and Mira met, about their falling in love, how he proposed to her, and what happened the night of the accident.I really enjoyed reading Danny’s POV and reading more about these characters.  They are a great group and I’ve come to enjoy Ashley’s writing a lot.  The story pretty much follows along with the story as told in Mirage until the end.  There’s an addition to the story that we didn’t see in Mirage.  While at the hospital visiting Mira, Danny meets a girl and he starts talking to her.  Then he starts thinking about her a little.  Not in a sexual way at all, but still.  The fact that this girl was brought into the story and that we already have is a love triangle thing going on here, makes you wonder where Ashley is going with this in the next book.  It would solve the whole Mira, Skylar, Danny issue if Danny meets someone else, but it did make me think Danny was a bit of an ass for talking to another girl while Mira was upstairs in a hospital bed in a coma.I have to say that while reading Mirage I never really became Team Danny or Team Skylar.  Danny and Mira were together and I felt bad for Skylar but I didn’t really root for one of them to end up with her versus the other.  After reading Inception, I am leaning towards Team Skylar.  Quite a few times in Inception Danny asked Skylar for advice or help when it came to Mira- like what to buy her or things to do for her.  And every time Skylar nailed it on the head.  He knew exactly what Mira would want or love.  He knows her so much better than Danny does and Danny needs to get a clue.  In terms of Skylar and his feelings for Mira, Danny did notice things that lead him to question if Skylar has feelings for Mira.  So at least he isn’t oblivious to the fact, which is good.Inception is a great novella to accompany Mirage, giving us insight into Danny’s mind and also giving us that little added part that makes you wonder what is going to happen in Awakening.  So between the big cliff hanger we were left with in Mirage and this new twist added here, I am ready to jump into Awakening.For more reviews go to [...]

reviewText: ***4 I-want-more stars!***While waiting for it to go live on Amazon and start syncing on my Kindle since I pre-ordered it months ago, this is me jumping up and down.Once it was on my Kindle, I started reading. The first few pages are kind of sad for me. I wasn't thinking how and why Grey was still a virgin and what made her desperate enough to start stripping so when I read her story, it made me sad. Emotional even. I couldn't say that I can relate with her situation but I've had some friends' parents who act and think just a little bit better than Grey's Daddy. It was suffocating. Unreasonable. Unfair. Even odd. So, I can only imagine Grey's life with a Dad like hers.The sadness didn't stop there.Her mom. Ohmygosh I cried reading about how Grey stood by her mother especially during her last breath."It's okay, Mama. I'll be okay. I'll miss you every day. But... you've fought so hard. I know you have. I know how much you love me and Daddy. I'll take care of him, okay? You... you can go now. It's okay. You don't have to fight anymore."HEARTBREAKING.OverviewGrey's Daddy is a pastor. An old-fashioned one at that. He believes almost everything is sinful - fashion, even movies and dancing - and women are supposed to stay at home and be all prim and proper."All Daddy cares about is his own idea of right and wrong. Everything is in black and white for him, and most things are black. There's more that's sinful and wrong than there are things that are okay."All the while I can imagine a terrible horror movie where the characters live in a haunted, deserted place and haven't seen and socialize with other people for years. Like they're stuck in the 1800's and we're now in 2013. Grey's Daddy is so closed-minded that he expects Grey to "marry a godly man headed for the seminary", she has to ask permission to dance and her Dad checks her steps and routine to make sure it isn't provocative or sinful, she grew sheltered and almost anti-social. It's admirable that Grey didn't turn out to be rebellious even just a little.Grey's Mom is supportive. She can be closed-minded too but it's more on just being agreeable to her Dad than it being what she really is. She was a dancer too but gave it up for Grey's Dad. She supports Grey's dancing but not very openly against Daddy and she still tells Grey to just follow what her Dad says and wants for her because it's for "her best". At the end though, I can feel her motherly love and support until she couldn't anymore."... I know... I know you may not want to be a pastor's wife, and I understand that."Reading about Grey's parents irritated me. I don't know what I expected Grey's story would be but being a sheltered pastor's daughter didn't cross my mind. After her Mom died, she packed up and left for L.A. even with her father somewhat disowning her for it.So she left for L.A. to pursue her college education in film with only $400 dollars in her name.And that's how the stripper story began...Grey AmundsenShe started struggling more after finding out that her grant is running out and she has to either use it all up or have it spread out until she finishes her degree but she has to pay for the remaining fees. So she started to look for jobs and because she was sheltered and have no work experience whatsoever, it was more difficult for her to land a job where she can get paid to afford her tuition, housing, and food expenses.Eyes closed, she decided that stripping is her only choice, she doesn't want to go back to her Dad in Georgia being a failure. She had to stand up for herself. Fend for herself. Work for her dream to be in the film industry. And stripping is the only available option for her at the time. So she goes for it.This part, and the few parts where she performs her strip routine, started to get slightly difficult for me to read mainly because I can feel she really doesn't want to do it, she's vulnerable, scared, alone, and she's trying to hold it all together and be strong."My breasts bounce free, and I stand topless in front of a hundred and fifty men.A single tear drips free to mingle with the sweat on my upper lip.I'm officially a stripper."Jasinda Wilder wrote it in a way where you can feel Grey's pain and struggle in being a stripper. I don't even know whether to feel sorry for her or I just want to say "If you're going to throw up and cry every time you finish your set, please for the love of God, JUST DON'T DO IT ANYMORE!!!"But then again, she's like a 13-year old girl, still lost in the world. Naive. So okay.Thank God for small blessings though because while working as a stripper at Exotic Nights, she met the famous, hot Hollywood actor, Dawson Kellor.There's instant attraction between Grey and Dawson. The way Dawson looked at Grey when she first entered the VIP room and how he asked the other men to leave when she started stripping felt intimate, passionate. And that kiss… sweet but not less hot."His mouth descends to mine, and his lips brush across mine, hot and moist and soft."Their sex scenes are hot, hot, hot but it's too bad it started happening way beyond halfway and almost nearing the end of the book.There were quite a few running, denials, and chasing that happens in this book but Dawson makes it worth it somehow. I like how he took over the job problem and the tuition after their argument about it. I get why Grey refuses to take it and sees it as her "being paid" but she could've handled it better and maybe came up with a compromise on her taking the money. She really doesn't like stripping, right?!After that incident, everything else happened too quickly for me. They were good and in love and Grey and her Daddy made peace, she moved in with Dawson, celebrated Dawson's birthday, Dawson proposed, and the Epilogue.If it wasn't well-written, I might have DNF-ed this. But it did work for me. Thankfully!OverallSo, that .5 is for the part where I want more and the other .5 is because I felt it's short (when it really isn't) and the good stuff happened slow and then fast and then it's done. Hence, the I want more part especially the Epilogue. You know I'm a sucker for those! :)
summary: If it wasn't well-written, I might have DNF-ed this. But thankfully, it worked out for me!

reviewText: Readers may be attracted by the curious title which could rate as one of the most imaginative of the year. However, it is perfectly apt for this Regency romance.Henrietta Watson, a young lady who delves rather too deeply into Mrs. Fairfax's dashing Gothic novels, is in love with her cousin Edward. As she's living in the depths of East Anglia, the mail coach only makes rare deliveries but, in Henrietta's world, Edward should be writing to her every day. And that's the problem - he's not, which isn't the behavior expected of a poetic lover. Then Henrietta discovers the reason: he's fallen in love with one of London's shining debutantes and is ready to elope with her. Henrietta has been relegated to past-lover status.Brokenhearted, she turns to her only confidante: her childhood friend and neighbor, Lord Kesseley who just happens to be every hot-blooded woman's dream: "shaggy chestnut curls...fell into his grey eyes...side-whiskers softened his otherwise hard, lean face". He tends to wear scruffy doeskins, smells of the barnyard and has been madly in love with Henrietta for years. He's the kind of man the reader wouldn't mind meeting on a dark, sultry night.On the other hand, Henrietta is not so endearing. She needs a good shake and a yell in the ear: "Wake up, woman, the guy loves you". After all, she's not stupid. She's able to answer her father's questions of "what is the distance from a center to a focus?" with barely a second's thought. Yet, it's all Edward, Edward, Edward and to get him back, she concocts the unlikely plot of transforming country-loving, down-to-earth Kesseley into one of her gothic heroes who will take London by storm, make the beautiful debutante fall out of love with Edward and into the arms of Kesseley. And, amazingly - given the man he is, he falls in with her plans, even going as far as to read her gothic romances so that he can get ideas. Is it hardly surprising that her brainless scheme works too well for her own good?The array of supporting characters are well portrayed, and the descriptions of houses, places and clothes are very well researched and on a par with any Jane Austen novel. If Henrietta could just be more convincing, the novel deserves four books. In fact I cared so little for her I was delighted when she fell flat on her face in Hyde Park. However, the plot races along with those all-intriguing questions lurking, "will she, won't she?" and "how will this get sorted out?" - perfect techniques for making the reader want to read on. But it's for Kesseley that I was most concerned. I just wanted the best for this man as he weaved in and out of the story.On the whole, despite some implausible plotting, the novel was well paced and, if you can bear just a couple of cheesy lines such as "Do you like me?" "Yes, can I touch you?" the love scenes were moving and satisfying. This is a feel-good book and, if you are interested in the culture and life-style of this era, and the fact there is one very likeable main character, then you'll enjoy the book.Originally posted at The Long and Short of It Romance Reviews

Reviewed by: LaciBook provided by: AuthorReview originally posted at Romancing the BookReview: I enjoyed A Dangerous Expectation, but I felt that there were scenes missing that could have filled in the story a little. It was an emotional tale that captured my heart. I found myself empathizing with Cassandra at first and later empathizing with Gray. They are both broken and in need of healing. This is a story that I think many people can relate to and understand.Cassandra is more than just a shut-in. She's become an agoraphobic. It's sad to find out that she feels such anxiety and terror in social situations that she just shuts down inside. She cares so much for her family that she retreats into herself to prevent anyone from getting mad at her and taking it out on her parents and siblings. That she meets her match in Gray is fantastic since he has his own personal demons to fight. He is also suffering but for a totally different reason, but he sees that she's broken and immediately makes the decision to help her, not knowing that in the end, he'll be helping himself as well. He comes to love her for herself and not for who she is or who she is related to.The couple of scenes that "fade to black", as I like to call it, are most likely meant to keep within the blush romance standards, but I feel like there could have been just a little more fill or explanation before it just ends and then when we flip the page, a whole new day starts. It made it feel a bit incomplete, like I was wanting more. It didn't have to break any of the rules of a blush romance, but the way it sharply ended made me flip back to see if I missed something. There were only two of those scenes that I got confused over, so it isn't enough to detract from the tone of the book. Overall, though, it was a good book and I enjoyed it. I give credit to the author for writing the heroine as an agoraphobic. I don't remember reading a heroine like that before.
summary: Emotional tale that captured my heart

reviewText: Jem Clayton is the orphaned son of a highly decorated and well-respected sheriff. He went astray and ended up on the opposite side of the law. In doing so, Jem developed a reputation of being a courteous bandit that never let harm come to a woman, and he was content to live that lifestyle. Unbeknownst to him, a more virtuous path awaited him.Jem's home town of Seneca 6 is a small, prosperous mining community that had existed peacefully for many years. After becoming entangled with a dangerous group of intergalactic outlaws known as The Harpe Gang, Jem puts Seneca 6 in a direct line of fire when they come looking for him.The Harpe Gang is unlike any force the universe had ever seen. Little Willy Harpe is a nasty human being with a penchant for cannibalism. He becomes even more deadly after taking possession of a "holy weapon"--a parasitic alien life form that bestows him with unprecedented power.Guns of Seneca 6 tells the tale of a man who fled from his past and now fights to reclaim it. Jem has plenty of help along the way as he battles a most formidable foe and uncovers a shocking secret that fills in the blanks regarding the demise of his father.Outlaws, savages, aliens, and a town under martial law: This is not the Wild West as you know it, and author Bernard Schaffer wouldn't have it any other way. While the inevitable comparisons to Firefly would be impossible to avoid, by time I closed the book, I found them to be two very different experiences.What they do share in common is a cast of strong characters that are so distinguishable and well-crafted that you could almost label any of them as the "main" character. Such an accomplishment has become Schaffer's signature. If you were to ask five different readers who their favorite character was, you're likely to get five different answers. For me, as much as I liked Jem Clayton, my favorite character was Doc Halladay.I have read all of Schaffer's books, and while each of them are fantastic reads, Guns of Seneca 6 stands out as my clear favorite. Answering why is a bit tough to explain. Guns possesses all of the trademark characteristics that comprise Schaffer's style, but the book feels more relaxed than his previous work. I didn't catch it until I was already a few chapters in, but it eventually dawned on me that there was a new rhythm to Schaffer's writing that I'd never noticed before. The flow of his sentence structure is cleaner and simpler to read.As much as I enjoyed Schaffer's last book, Whitechapel: The Final Stand of Sherlock Holmes, it was an exhausting read. It read more like a technical writing manual and took me about two weeks to finish. Guns will enable readers of any level to feel entertained and less challenged. It's structured in a way that allows you to just enjoy the story while subliminally giving you a lesson in how to write effectively.Even as I was rounding the corner near the end of Guns, I was already envisioning where Schaffer may take the story next. I don't doubt for a second that he's got a list of notes for a sequel, and I'm anxious to reach the day when I can enjoy that one too. For now, if you're not already a fan of Schaffer, you should be. I can't think of a better introduction to what makes his work great than Guns of Seneca 6.

In a nutshell, if you liked City of Rogues, you'll likely enjoy this as well.  Kron Darkbow is on the road with Adara, master swordswoman, and Randall, a nice young man who happens to be the son of a depraved, evil super-wizard.  They're hunted by the villains they failed to finish off in City of Rogues, stalked by war demons sent by the villain they're after in the next book, and they're facing all sorts of new villains all along the road.The same strengths from City of Rogues are in place in Road to Wrath.  There is non-stop action, a bit of struggle with moral dilemmas, a dark theme of vengeance and justice, and then even more action.The same weaknesses are present as well.  Some of the writing is clumsy, and there are some irritating typos.  None of it is very deep, in characterization or world-building.  However, the power of the storytelling makes the book irresistible.

Eric had to get out of the safehouse. He couldn't stand it for one more minute.That's how he finds himself in the alley with the woman. Not sure if she's spotted him yet, he slips deeper into the shadows.He'd first spotted her in the club. they exchanged passing glances. He should've known the night was going to be bad when he thought he saw her again at the next club.When he spots her in the shadows of a doorway outside, his worry turns to dread.Sure enough, she follows him, so he ducks into the alley to hide.But she follows him.She calls out to him."Come on out and play, you little b...."She casually steps forward as Eric slips further down the alley, and her hand, when she withdraws it from her coat, holds a gun.Not good.This was fun. At first I thought Eric was one thing, then I thought he was another. It was fun finding out what he was or wasn't and whether he was a good guy or a bad guy. I'll let you draw your own conclusions about that.You know that feeling you get where the hair stands up on the back of your neck and you're sure someone or something is watching you? That's what I experienced when reading Out After Dark. I'm sure that's how the author wanted me to feel. Good job creeping me out.When the true story of the mysterious woman became clear, I was delighted. I had it somewhat figured out, but then Brandon did the twists thing again, and took it in another direction. An exciting one too!I just wish it had been longer!Four Stars for Out After Dark!

reviewText: I suffered 4 years of chronic major depression after a cancer operation 6 years ago. So I'm interested in stress relief topics - especially ones I can implement quickly if I feel the need to head off arising stress. There were some techniques in this book I knew, but there were also some I had no idea about. What makes this book valuable is its clarity and simple presentation of the 12 techniques - making it a quick reference tool when needed.

A five star book!!  This steamy story by Miranda E. Kopps is an awesome read.  Tessie is just trying to find happiness.  She tries to keep her very religious Mother and Father happy by staying with a man her parents adore.  Sadly, Clarence is an abusive cop Tessie feels trapped with.  In need of a friend and someone to talk with, Tessie meets her neighbor Chloe.  After several coffee dates, Tessie finds herself thinking thoughts about Chloe and feeling feelings she has never experienced before.  She is lost and confused.  Tessie is finally forced to make a decision that will change her life forever.  Will she choose a life with Clarence, a life she has always known? A life she knows her parents want for her.  Or, will she choose a life that will make her be true to herself?  I look forward to reading more books by Miranda E. Kopps.  I highly recommend this book.

I found the world building in both stories to be very intriguing, although the second story was really just a snippet and we were only given a fleeting glimpse of a world I would love to read more about. (M/M in this one) I liked it a bit better than the first story actually and I hope Leigh will be writing a longer story about these characters.Leigh has a wonderful imagination! Let's just put that out there first of all. I think she tried putting a bit too much into such short stories but I have to commend her for the shear breadth of the worlds she is building. It's going to be very interesting to see where she goes with the characters in both stories. I will however, be waiting until she finishes writing them all and they are compiled in a bundle as I dislike reading serial stories with cliffhangers. The cliffhanger at the end of the first story wasn't as horrible as cliffhangers usually are. The MCs did have a satisfactory HFN ending after all. Most of the secondary characters were quite well fleshed out and I would like to see where they are headed. The second story didn't actually have an ending, it just stops.The first story has so much in it, including many more folklore based characters than just the usual werewolves and vampires. The world of these people is accessed through portals that certain people can open and the world is based on our world so things like buildings in cities line up in unusual ways. You aren't quite sure just who the bad guys are and even by the end of the story there is some confusion about just who the bad guys ultimately are. There isn't a lot more I can say without adding spoilers.The points of the story that need work; there is so much information that it can be a bit confusing at times; the sex scenes themselves are quite steamy, but sometimes start rather abruptly; sometimes the dialog flowed well and others it seems rather forced; there were a lot of unanswered questions that I hope will be addressed in the next book.Because of these I couldn't quite give it 4 stars, in fact if the ideas and characters weren't so fabulous I might have only given it 2 stars because I found parts of the story to be irritating, but the fact is that I really liked the storyline and the characters a lot so I will be reading more in this series to see what happens to them.In short, if you are easily confused and/or irritated, you might want to give this book a miss. However, if you can deal with that, this book will get your imagination revved up. Finding so many different ideas in one place can be both challenging and exhilarating.

reviewText: Best Freaking Book in the series! !Ooooh Lili, what are you doing to me?? My heart, my poor poor heart. You've outdone yourself with Five Miles. I was hurting, I was panting, and I was scared. You made my heart melt with Elliot, and you broke my heart at the end with Jase -sigh... freaking perfect.If you loved Seven Sons & Six Brothers you'll be over the moon with Five Miles. Nope, I'm not fan-girling, it's the god damn truth!I can't give away too much and can only advice you read my previous reviews and def start this series!! It's one of the best novella series I've ever read.Sammi was awesome and I got to know her even better in book 3, and I've no idea how she's holding on but she has my utter respect. She faces the ugly and painful truth every damn day when being with Dornan (<-- yep I still hate his guts, now even more!)."Here's what I have learned from living with the devil: It's not enough to simply do what he says. It's not enough at all. To keep him distracted, you both have to believe the lie." ...oh and she does..He's his usual disgusting, brutal, and lethal self and I despise him. Dornan is sick and I'd be scared endless in Sammi's place. Five Miles starts off where Six Brothers ended -Sammi in the hospital where she takes a night trip to Elliot.Oooh Elliot, I'm torn between you and Jase because I feel you; I truly do. Sammi and his flashbacks were sugar sweet and painful to read to the same time. " 'Elliot," I whispered, 'I'm in love with you.' His eyes searched mine, glassy and worried. I swallowed thickly. 'Do you - do you feel like this, too?' He nodded slowly."I understand him so well why he wants her out of this nightmare. He can't stand hearing what she's doing and accepts what Dornan is doing to her -aaaagh, me neither! He's struggling with everything -past and presents colliding with each other: "All I wanted was you, Julz. ... I shouldn't have left you. I'm sorry. Every day, I think about you. What might have been." Do you hear that?? This was my heart breaking for him/them.Then there's Jase, her love. The only brother she can't seem to fool, hurt, or lie to. It is eating her slowly alive and oh gosh I could sooo feel her suffering (damn Lili, I blame you lol). The weight on her shoulders is slowing but surely dragging her down. "It's almost like dying...little by little; piece by piece. Burnt out, shattered, breaking apart under the weight of my lies - and I still have five to go.""You can lie to the boy you've loved since you were fifteen years old, but that doesn't mean he'll believe you. ..."This was again, one crazy ride and I can't believe the plan she had this time -thanks to Elliot. You'd think, BAM, problem solved,nope...not one bit. Dornan seems indestructible.But that's not the only thing what happened while trying to bring them down... some brothers are not as stupid as she thought and she's walking on thin ice... so thin that my heart was literally hammering out of my chest.Just read this book!! The ending...OMG!!...that's all I'm saying."His lips leave my mouth and trail hot, wet kisses down my neck. 'I'll stop,' he gasps between kisses. 'You say stop and I'll stop, I swear to you.' .... 'Don't stop.' ... "**COPY GIFTED**

To start off, this is not a full-length book but the second of a ten-part series of short stories: it will take you less than an hour to read this one and, of the ten stories, this is probably the weakest one as it is just too short and leaves you really hanging wanting more and is a little incomplete.  If you haven't read the first book of the series (Renewal without any of the numbers after it), you need to read that one first then progress in numerical order through #10.Similar to the other books in the series, the author sets you into a futuristic (and believable) outlook of America several decades after a nuclear destruction of organized society, with frequent flashbacks / narrations of what happened immediately after to the surviving families.  I could actually visualize the various scenes and situations, and found myself wondering "what if" or "what would I do" while reading not only this one, but the other stories in the series.  The author does a good job of wetting your tastebuds and wanting a little more at the conclusion of the story - hence, let's go purchase the next book  of the series.  Overall, the series is very good and I highly recommend it.I will point out I did read all ten of the stories of the series and, while good, it was a little annoying to having just strapped myself in to read for a while then finding the various stories ended and I had to go buy another.  Mr. Perkins, if you are reading this review I would encourage you to put all ten stories into one edition and raise the price - your readers will thank you for it (and spend less money) while you will make more off of the 70% royalty!
summary: Good Series - Chapter 2 Leaves You Really Hanging

reviewText: I have never read a self-help book before. I'm glad my first experience of one was Dolores Ayotte's Up the 'Down' Ladder. This book was brilliant. Ayotte offers help through a friendly, comfortable manner. It feels as if you are taking advice from a close and wise friend. This book is about dealing with depression, and how the first step of dealing with it is not to ignore the problem and not to feel ashamed with accepting the truth that in this moment you are depressed but that it is correctible.Ayotte draws the reader in, you realise that she suffered depression and through her you understand that it can happen to anyone but so long as you approach it in the right way, you can get better. You can get up the 'Down' ladder. You accompany her on her journey, which is often sprinkled with humour. This is a book worth reading, and one you should always keep on a shelf, just in case.

reviewText: This is a really good book, and the latest in the Vin Cooper series. The action and plot are great, and it is fun to read.  And as usual, Cooper kicks some serious butt!If I had any criticism at all, it would be the usual problem with action books.....the unreality, couldn't be real problem. Rollins does a good job with this, cuts it close and it is mostly at least barely believable.  Now, since the story concerns a stolen US nuke, one could say that having such a small recovery team is a bit ridiculous. We all know if a nuke went missing, US special forces would kill anyone and everyone they had to to get it back.  There'd be thousands deployed and they would never stop. In this case, we have Cooper and a couple of others, against the terrorists. But, Rollins again does a nice job of explaining why it happened like this.All in all I really enjoyed reading War Lord.

Sarah Dalton has written a big twist on the beauty pageant mentality. The girl we are usually led to hate comes across as much more, with courage and conviction to make any mother proud. Too bad Elena's mother is so wrapped up in her own rounds of maintaining the beauty that nature had nothing to do with.This is a story of cloning taken to an ugly conclusion. Pairing genetic material to produce perfectly beautiful children failed to produce people with intelligence and heart. Elena breaks the mold of self-absorbed beauty queen. She's guilt-ridden for the years she spent bullying the Blemished (natural born people) who are relegated to lives of squalor and servitude to the ruling clone class.This is book #1 in a series. The chemistry between the hero and heroine was off the charts hot. The witty and sarcastic dialogue kept me smiling. Also, this story is more character driven rather than action driven, meaning there are no bad guys to fight. However, make no mistake, the story is tremendously good! I started reading this book just during my lunch breaks and all the mythology and world building was so overwhelming. I had a hard time keeping up with everything and remembering it all. Then I decided to switch to reading it at home so after I finished the book I was currently reading I picked this back up. Reading this in longer pieces at a time was much better, so I definitely recommend reading this in fewer sittings. The story is much more enjoyable that way. I know this is the first in a series and the main character had to discover all these secrets and her abilities, but the plot moved very slowly until the last portion of the book. That might be another reason I struggled with it at first. It still needs more polish and editing to fix the word use issues and some grammatical errors (for example conscious was used instead of the correct word conscience). Overall I think this is a pretty interesting story of magic and discovery. I love the idea of the Seer narrating. The book reads mostly in third person but every now and then we're reminded of the invisible to most viewer and teller of the story. I like that this fairy tale is "vanity's war" and includes a magic mirror. The cover is also really pretty and conveys the vanity/mirror aspect. I enjoy stories using the 7 deadly sins in the plot so I'm definitely interested in continuing the series.

Dragonfly Kisses is the 2nd book in the amazing Tryst Island series by Sabrina York.  For any of you that read my review for Rebound you know that I was already hooked on this series just one book into it.  Dragonfly Kisses sealed the deal.  It offers the same witty, smart dialogue and super hot sex scenes, with an added element of a heartwrenching past to overcome.The Tryst Island series is set up around a group of college friends.  2 of the friends own a big beautiful house on the Island; the others all share the utilities and living expenses.  The house is used as a getaway whenever an individual or the group wants to escape life and it's demands or just have a great fun filled weekend.Dylan Deveney is ready to give up on life.  Love and attraction isn't even a blip on his radar.  He's alone at the Island house nursing his depression and contemplating ending it all.  And then he hears the voice of an angel.  Okay, maybe not an angel, more like the girl staying in the house across from him, but whatever.  Seeing her sends a punch to his stomach that he's never felt before.  It's just too bad he has no idea who she is and he's just not emotionally up to chasing after her at the moment.  But, something about her keeps him hanging on.  He sees her several times over the next several months and each time it's the same feeling.  Then one day fate intervenes and his angel is thrown into his life, now he just has to trust that things will work out as they should.Cassie French couldn't be more shocked when she meets her island neighbor.  Her roommates have been going crazy over him for months, but she has had no interest in ogling the guy like they do.  Finally, she gives in to their insistant demands and goes with them to "coincidentally" run into him while he's jogging.  After all, 2 of her friends are vying for his attention and they need an impartial party.  So, why is it when she sees him she immediately wants to smack her friends for fawning over him and claim him for herself?  He is nowhere near her type.  He's far too masculine and wild looking - not the normal "safe" guy she goes for.  Dyaln stumbles literally into her life.  He hurt his ankle and she just happens to be skilled in first aid.  While delivering him crutches he admits that he knows who she is and that he's been to her concerts and loves to hear her play her cello.  The sparks fly, but Cassie fears that her friends will never forgive her for falling for the guy they are interested in.  Throwing caution to the wind she enjoys a passion filled weekend that changes her life.This book is filled with so much emotion my heart literally hurt for both characters.  Dylan has suffered a huge loss and doesn't think he can ever bear to go through it, again.  Cassie loves her family, but is tired of living the life that they expect her to live.  The journey they take to overcome their problems and to have a chance at a happy future is heartbreaking at times, but heartwarming and sweet.This book was provided to me in exchange for my honest review.You can find this review and others at [...] and [...]

I loved S. R. Mallery's first book, Unexpected Gifts, for its rich and varied historical eras used in the setting and theme of the novel.She continues that same talent in her collection of short stories, Sewing Can Be Dangerous and Other Small Threads. The thread that holds the stories together is a literal one as all the short stories employ some type of sewing or weaving of threads at the heart of the plots. The stories are set in important historical eras and are sometimes romantic, sometimes horrific, and always riveting. The life of immigrants who worked in the textile plants during the heyday of the Industrial Revolution are profiled in one of the short stories. It's not only an indictment of the appalling conditions of the workrooms but Ms. Mallery also examines the yearnings of a young woman who wants to disappear from her cruel and repressive father. Nazi Germany and all its ramifications on those who tried to help the Jews escape from the torture and death at the hands of the Nazis is the setting for one story. A quilt becomes the all important piece of evidence and hope for fifty Jews hoping to leave the country before they were rounded up by Hitler's soldiers. Medieval courts, Hopi and Chinook native traditions, the sixties from a unique perspective, and more make up the varied and entertaining plots.In the talented hands of Ms. Mallery, this collection of short stories allows the reader to escape into other worlds where even a macrame necklace can become an object of subterfuge and a piece of evidence in a murder case.I thoroughly enjoyed reading each story. I began each one with great anticipation as I discovered the era, setting, and threads to tie it altogether. Sometimes the sewing and thread of the story wasn't evident, and in other stories, it played a starring role.The divergent historical content is impressive. Ms. Mallery's research is evident only after completing the story because while engrossed in the plot of each one, I forgot I was reading and simply enjoyed each of the journeys Ms. Mallery created for me.I highly recommend reading this collection of short stories weaved by a very meticulous and talented author.

reviewText: The moment I read the book description, I knew that I had to get “Vanished from Dust”. I’ve always liked the idea of small towns that hide dark secrets and terrible past events, so I had to know what was with the mysterious death of hundreds of townspeople in 1922. I have to admit that the author didn’t disappoint me in the least. Of course, I don’t intend to spoil the mystery for you, so you’ll have to read the book to find out what happened in Dust, Texas, the town Eric and his best friend, Kyle, are from.The novel begins with quite a powerful scene: Eric is bullied by his classmates because he said that he can see phantoms. Everyone thinks he is crazy, so what they do is beat him, insult him, and call him names. The only one who stands up for Eric is Kyle, who is the new kid in town. I’ve always liked young adult novels that prove to be more than just fun and entertaining. “Vanished from Dust” touches on the problematic matter of bullying, and it portrays it in a very realistic way. Then, the author emphasizes the strong friendship between Eric and Kyle, and how much it means to them.I loved that the characters were very well developed, likeable, and believable. This adds a lot to the story, which is also filled with mystery, suspense, and unexpected twists. All these elements kept me glued to the pages, and I managed to read the novel in two sittings. I would recommend it to readers of all ages, even if the description says it is a paranormal novel for young adults.

Edwin Stark is a writer who, as he would say, is trapped in the hinterlands of Venezuela. This would be terrible if it hadn't inspired him to write the uproarious romp known as "Eco Station One."Eduardo Sinnombre is a man struggling to survive in the financial wasteland that Venezuela has become, so when he stumbles across a help wanted ad for a job that offers a fabulous wage, he lurches toward the chance. But from the moment he meets corpulent job offerer Thaddeus T. Barnum, representative of the evil Mucusoft software company, he knows he's stepping into a huge muck hole. That knowledge, however, doesn't dissuade him from accepting the cash--er, position.And so Eduardo journeys all the way to Eco Station One, a scientific outpost positioned ever-so-inconveniently in the rainforest, which is also smack dab in the center of Ikawiri Pigmy territory. As if having to sing his way past the vicious natives weren't bad enough, Eduardo soon finds that his guide Pedro Alfredo Mendoza dela Villahuerta Paomos y Linarez (Mendoza for short) has it in for him, and with the help of his three cousins Taco, Paco, and Manolo (the Mendoza Trio) it seems almost certain Mendoza will sabotage his new job.Populated by wacky events and zany characters (which include Harry the talking--well, signing--black mountain gorilla and Paul Culvert the bus-driving hippy who still thinks he's in the 1970s), "Eco Station One" is sure to grab you by the armpits and tickle you mercilessly right up until the last page.Read this book and enjoy a story that is as hilarious as the Stark-raving voice that tells it.
summary: South America will never be the same...

reviewText: Quinn has had some pretty bad things happen in her past that have formed who she is currently.  She has problems with trusting people, isn’t looking for a relationship, doesn’t believe in love at this time, and has severe panic attacks that affect her life.  Her answer to relationships is Tyler Claiborne (Talented Twisted Tyler).  He was what she thought was her type of man; he was in a band, worked as a bartender at Strikers, had tattoos and didn’t do relationships.  Their relationship was an agreement to have sex, friends with benefits.  One Friday night a man to be known as Preppy Porter tried to make conversation with her and she very rudely shut him down.Reed Porter was a blond, athletic, environmentalist, who also had some skeletons in his closet that caused him to shy away from relationships as well.  He had been hurt and cheated on and didn’t want to put himself out there again.  So when he met Quinn at Strikers, he didn’t know what to think except she was being a complete bitch to him.Neither Quinn nor Reed had any idea what fate had in store for them.  This is a story of two heartbroken people, who run into each other by accident, not looking for anything, but they can’t deny there is something out there for them; they just don’t want to accept it.This book has amazing HOT and Sensual sex scenes, a journey of self discovery for Quinn and the very important lesson in life that just because you aren’t looking for love, it might find you anyway.  Quinn at times was one of the most frustrating characters that I have dealt with, I literally found myself talking to her when she was making stupid moves or saying things that made absolutely no sense.  She was the queen of self-sabotage when it came to her life and relationships.  I definitely was rooting for Reed, it came across as that all around American guy, but he still had is Alpha male side in the bedroom.Lisa Suzanne you have done it again.  This book was EXCELLENT.  I enjoyed every minute of it, you made me laugh, cry, yell and argue with Quinn.  I was sad to see it end, but happy to read that you are going to have another book with character from this one.  

Great great story of second chances.  Elle was literally pulled from the arms of her boyfriend by her creepy father when she was younger.  She never gave Her boyfriend Prentice a real explanation why she was suddenly leaving him, only saying it was all a mistake that they would be engaged and that it would never work between them.  Fast forward 20 years, Elle and Prentice find themselves reuniting for their mutual friend's wedding.  During the 20 year separation, both of them had married others and, in Elle's case, a marriage of convenience fell apart, and for Prentice, a good marriage ended when his wife suffered a brain tumor and died, leaving him a widower with 2 beautiful young children.  Their initial reunion was not a good experience, especially for Elle, as Prentice had obviously never gotten over the way she left him so many years earlier.  The story continues and we see how both have spent 20 years moving through life, but never really getting past the true love that they had as young lovers.  Prentice's approach was to be mean and he tried to be distant with Elle.  You couldn't help but feel sorry for Elle because really she had no choice when she left Prentice, she had a horribly mean and abusive father and in the 20 years since abandoning Prentice, she had suffered both physical, verbal and emotional abuse at the hands of her father and her rich arrogant husband.  All and all this story took us through watching Prentice and Elle fight to deny their true feelings and then fight to act on their true feelings.  It was an emotional roller coaster as they could both be very stubborn people.  The secondary characters of their friends and family were really great, most especially Prentice's children, and his ghost of a wife, Fiona, and Elle's friend Mikey. Loved this book and as always, Kristen Ashley never ceases to amaze.  I loved all her bad boy books, and loved all the Rock Chicks, and didn't really think I would like the "fantasy" books, but boy was I wrong.  This series, Ghosts and Reincarnations is awesome.  We still get the alpha males she does sooooo well, the beautiful and smart heroines, the strong family and friends, and always hot hot love scenes, all with a bit of whimsy.  Highly recommend this series and anything Kristen Ashley.

This book started out very promising with three friends reconnecting after 10 years apart, but time changes everyone... or has it really? Some deception and manipulation leads to some issues for these three, but I liked the clear communication the author was stressing with the complex relationship these characters were trying to have. They approached it very honestly with real issues, but at times it felt like it was almost too much. Liam and Kat were a bit too willing to uproot their lives (although Liam eventually has some issues), and Hunter was completely uncompromising with his life to include them in it. It felt like he was trying to talk them out of it at every turn to the point where I didn't even think he wanted them for anything beyond sex. Although he was stating real potential issues for the future, it just felt like he had no give whatsoever to include them in his life and I didn't see that working out for the three of them in the long run. Now the heat between the characters was good, but I have to say that it just always seemed so rushed. We get these intense feelings all being drawn out into the open and they engage in plenty of sex, but I didn't feel any real emotion in the act. Just as the relationship starts to form, we just get a drop off type of ending leaving details lingering on how things work out. I realize things won't be resolved overnight and that they have a long road ahead, but it just made the story feel incomplete for me. I have to say that overall the book had some good points leaving me wanting more, but unfortunately not in a good way.*I received a review copy of this from the publisher via NetGalley in exchange for my honest review*

I was somewhat intrigued by the story line and then persuaded by the great reviews.  I just can't agree with them.  This is an OK little story that felt more like one at the YA level and would have really benefited from a lot of editing:1) There are "highfalutin" words used occasionally that don't make any sense in the context in which they are used.  My guess is that they were selected from a thesaurus in an attempt to make the writing sound sophisticated.  I can't think of an example right now, and I didn't write them down as I came across them, but a simpler, less "sophisticated" synonym (probably the original word) would have made much more sense.2) A phrase that is obviously a favorite of the author's but is extremely over-used is "in all."  It is often used several times in just a few paragraphs.  I am normally a pretty forgiving reader and can usually overlook a lot, but after a while I found it quite distracting.3) A character exclaims, "by all that's wholly!"  Uh?  I assume the author meant, "by all that's holy."  There's really no excuse for missing an error like that.4) The story switches from 1st person to 3rd person and back again within a couple of paragraphs, within the same scene, and with the same character.5) Then there are grammatical problems, words that are just left out, etc. and the reader is left to try to make sense of the sentence.6) Emotions are extreme (that particularly made it feel like a YA story).  And there is no explanation for the way Kela is treated by her grandfather -- we're told he hates her, he glares at her, he thinks she's a weakling, others have to secretly help her or incur his wrath, he accepts her siblings but refuses to acknowledge her as his granddaughter, etc.  But then we're expected to believe that, even though she's being treated so badly, he's doing what he thinks is best for her.7) The setting, characters and plot are not fleshed out at all, and many opportunities to do so are missed.  The only exception to this is the protagonist, Kela. Very little is revealed about the different societies mentioned, the other characters, their powers, the enemy, why Kela is treated the way she is, etc.  In fact, so little is revealed that I really have no desire to continue reading the story in Part Two to find out more.

reviewText: I have been a huge fan pf Preston's work since I read the first page of No More Wasted Time. The Mathews family will always hold  a place in my heart. I even enjoyed twenty-first century Harry's emotional growth and how he treated Stella while she was in the coma. In fact, I loved everything about the story until I got to the end. The end completely blew me away, and not in a good way. I will not give the ending away, but suffice it to say that the author did a fantastic job of building the story up to the end, and then...leaving the reader hanging with no solutions to any of the problems presented by the story. It was like having a balloon be blown up and you are waiting for it to explode and rain confetti on you, and instead the air rushes out with a low whistle and that is it. That was a huge disappointment for me as a reader and that alone lowered the rating down to a 3 cup from a 5 cup. Now, that being said, this is still a good book, and very easy to read, and I did enjoy it, I just was not happy with the ending. If you enjoy reading about past civilizations, and pondering the idea of alternate realities and timelines, out of body experiences and these sorts of things then for those I can heartily recommend this book, it is worth reading.ReginaReviewer for Coffee Time Romance & More

reviewText: Charlie has a huge gambling debt, but fortunately he’s offered a chance to clear his debt. Charlie thinks his luck is turning, but the ship has a long history of suicide, violence, murder, mutiny, and basically, every bad thing under the sun. If he’s to get out of there alive, he’ll need more than just luck.Deadlock is another excellent piece of dark fiction by one of my favorite publishers, DarkFuse. This isn’t my first time reading a book by Tim Curran, and I doubt it’ll be the last. Tim Curran always manages to paint a grim, groomy, atmospheric and claustrophobic story that focuses on one man, one haunted ship, and the man’s descent into madness during his night on board.It’s not as straightforward as the synopsis would want you to assume, and this novella shows that the true monster can be hidden well, and one should not always fear the ghouls crawling from one’s closet, when there are things out there more wicked than any ghoul. While atmospheric for the most part, there’s plenty of gore toward the end, with vivid descriptions that made me picture the scenes in detail (sometimes too much detail).An excellent read, highly recommended to all horror fans. I received a free copy of this book in exchange for an honest review.

reviewText: Success fades into oblivion, and failure--if used cleverly to fire your ambition--to eventual success. This story presents Terry Sparkes, a has-been actor whose face no longer adores the billboards. For as long as he can remember, he has felt the need to play a role. Most of all, he pretends to himself these days, thinking himself a celebrity despite that fact that he is no longer in the public eye. "At least he was still working and that, according to Terry Sparkes at least, constituted success.The story is set over the course of a Oscar night, during which Hollywood would give recognition to its finest thespians, and one of the contenders for whom Terry and others across Britain are rooting for is one of the world's greatest actors: Sir Michael. His name is in the limelight, much in opposition to his fan, Terry Sparkes, who has fallen into the shadows of obscurity. It is from there that he hopes to get the vicarious thrill of success. As the ceremony plays on his TV, his mind flashes back to his own past, back in the time he has won a role in the BBC's most popular soap opera. "Everywhere he went he was stopped in the street and asked for his autograph... His star was shining bright." Until, that is, the soap opera was axed, and Terry can barely find work anymore, because of having been typecast by it. Perhaps he should not have accepted that role in the first place, because it reduced him from being a character actor to a one-dimensional `bad-boy'.The author, Duncan Whitehead, invites us to compare the path of the two actors. They are similar in every way, so the only thing that separates them is their luck: "They were both sixty years of age and each had begun acting at roughly the ams time... Both actors were tall men and they each had striking features, coupled with neatly cropped dark hair."As the Oscar ceremony comes to it height, Terry sparkes sustains his attention by snorting some white powder. Will Terry come to realize that his meteoric rise inevitably brought about his fall?  Will he hear Sir Michael's acceptance speech, upon receiving the golden statuette? Will he realize that it includes a tribute to one special man? Will he reflect upon the connection between the rise of one of them and the decline of the other--or is this reflection left, in the end, only to us?Five stars.

At this point I am just over 60% of the way through and so annoyed I needed to stop reading.  Firstly, this tale could have been set in any time period, very few Regency specific references, so I would not say it fit the Recency category - although that is the least of my problems with it.  Secondly, and most importantly, there is no excuse for a romantic hero to be constantly kissing his employee.  This is not romance..this is immaturity and lack of self control (he is in his 30s and she is 19).  I don't care if he thinks he wants to marry her.  She is still works for him and is wholly dependent on his good will.  I suppose the author thinks we are supposed to be so distracted by the idea of love/lust at first sight that we ignore this fact and see it as basic, clumsy courting since he only kisses her.  If this hero were as wonderful as we are supposed to think he is he would be able to control his basic urges and work out the issues keeping him from offering for her!  Or just go ahead and make her his mistress.The author is not a bad writer.  She does know how to tell a story although the overlong dialog does become arduous.  I might try another of her books to see if it suffers the same annoyances however, if one wants to read great, romantic stories involving  governesses  and their employers I would highly recommend any of Deborah Hale's books.  As I have unfortunately read all of hers, I was hoping this would be as satisfying.  Instead I am angry at my wasted time.

Opening lines:  ‘…There were three things in life Jaime Josephina Hanrahan couldn’t stand.  Her name, public transport and musclebound men riding Harley-Davidsons.  She couldn’t do much about the first, unfortunately. And the last two were currently in her line of vision.…’You have a fair idea that you are going to enjoy a book when a non-romance reading friend of yours recommends it.  She was right, I really enjoyed A BUSH CHRISTMAS.Jaime is heading into the East Gippsland highlands region of the Australian to avoid Christmas.  She has just been retrenched, it is her first Christmas without her beloved father and her mother has gone off her rocker (Jaime’s opinion) and remarried a man who is the complete opposite to her father in every way.  She is not happy.  Jaime accepts a job housesitting in the remote bush as she is sure it will be easy to avoid Christmas.She soon finds out that Christmas is everywhere, and her near neighbour, the musclebound man who was riding the Harley, is decorating the property from top to bottom.  Station Manager, Stirling McEvoy, does not like city girls and he is not impressed with Jaime, and he can’t understand how anyone can hate Christmas so much. Firstly he thought that Jaime was going to be a male and help run the property while the owner is away.  And secondly she is pretty little bombshell with clothes more appropriate for the beach than a working.  But Jaime is a tough little cookie and not one to stay away from hard work.  She takes everything that Stirling throws at her including manually separating the cattle, and holding the spotlight while he shoots rabbits despite the fact she believes he is murdering all the little Thumpers in cold blood. I can actually relate to this one, any years ago spending a weekend on a NSW bush property with an ex-boyfriend’s mate who took us spotlighting for kangaroo. I thought that we were looking for them just so they could show me them, I didn’t realise the spotlight caused them to freeze on the spot so they were easy to shoot! I kept turning the spotlights off at the last minute until seething with rage the property owner drove me back to the station and made me get out while the boys all went off without me.  I now understand that this was not an idle sport for the property owner – but the knowledge came too late and my name was mud!  Getting back to Jaime, she even rises to the challenge when the local ladies steamroll her into promising to cook umpteen sponge cakes when she can’t so much as successfully cook a packet mix!  Christmas day dawns with Jaime’s mother and husband along with everyone from miles around descending onto the property to celebrate Christmas.  What is a girl who hates Christmas to do?A BUSH CHRISTMAS is a wonderfully funny and romantic Christmas rural romance. A quick and easy read that shows that you don’t have to have snow to let the magic of Christmas get working and for two lonely people find a common ground for love to grow.

reviewText: This book is by no means a tour guide, but rather a compilation of the author’s suggestions as to some of the most interesting places the Earth has to offer. Children and adults who are interested in geography, culture, history, archeology or nature will all find something of interest in this book. Morris organizes the book by continents. He then chooses some very well known sites as well as some that are obscure. Unfortunately, there are no pictures, but the author offers a link to investigate pictures of those sites that most interest the reader. This work is a great reference book and a good place to look for interesting ideas and places to explore.I will give a few examples to whet your appetite. On the continent of Asia, one of the largest wonders is The Great Wall of China. The two thousand year old wall served as military protection as well as a means of transportation of trade known as the Silk Wall. I had never heard of Panjin Red Beach which is covered with thousands of red sea weeds and is a home to hundreds of species of animals and birds. In Europe, you can visit the popular tourist sites like the Eiffel Tower in Paris, the Leaning Tower of Pisa or the ruins in Athens. Then there is the little known Sedlec Ossuary or Bone Chapel in the Czech Republic which is made of forty to seventy thousand sets of human bones or the Ice Hotel in Sweden which is built from ice harvested from the Torne River and reconstructed every year between December and April. In North America millions of tourists have visited the Grand Canyon and Disney World, but fewer have traveled to Antelope Canyon opened in 1997. South America s noted for the ruins of Machu Picchu and Angel Falls, but not many have visited the Enchanted Well or The Swing at the End of the World. In Oceania tourists visit the Sydney Opera House and the Great Barrier Reef, but fewer numbers venture to the Glow Worm Beach. The continent of Africa offers the Pyramids of Giza, Victoria Falls and Table Mountain.For those not satisfied with keeping their feet firmly planted on the ground, The Virgin Galactic is a space craft offering suborbital travel for the price of $250,000. Whatever your time or budget, this guide will allow you to be an armchair traveler to some of the most interesting sites on the planet!
